//Example 1.8.// We have the following examples of strict categories.

  * The strict category \(\mathcal{Set}\) of sets and functions.
  * The strict category \(\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\) of pointed sets and basepoint-preserving functions.
  * For a field \(k\), the strict category \(\mathcal{Vect}_k\) of \(k\)-vector spaces and \(k\)-linear maps.
  * The strict category \(\mathcal{Top}\) of topological spaces and continuous functions.

All these strict categories are locally small, but not small.

**Definition 1.9.** Let \(\mathcal C\) be a strict category. A morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) is an **isomorphism** if there is a morphism \(g:y\to x\) in \(\mathcal C\) such that \(g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_x\) and \(f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_y\). We write \(f:x\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}y\) or \(f:x\cong y\). We call \(g\) an **inverse** of \(f\).

We say that two objects \(x\) and \(y\) in \(\mathcal C\) are **isomorphic** if there is an isomorphism \(f:x\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}y\) in \(\mathcal C\). We write \(x\cong y\).

**Proposition 1.11.** //Let \(\mathcal C\) be a strict category. An isomorphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) has a unique inverse, which we denote by \(f^{-1}:y\to x\).//
proof_dokuwiki:
//Proof.// Suppose that \(g,h:y\to x\) are two inverses of \(f\) in \(\mathcal C\). Then

$$g=g\circ\operatorname{id}_y=g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h=\operatorname{id}_x\circ h=h.\quad\square$$

**Definition 1.12.** Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), a **functor** \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) consists of:

  * a function \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)\) sending an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to an object \(Fx\in\mathcal D\);
  * for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), a function \(\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)\) sending a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to a morphism \(Ff:Fx\to Fy\) in \(\mathcal D\);

satisfying the following axioms:

  * \(F\) preserves identities: for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\),

$$F(\operatorname{id}_x)=\operatorname{id}_{Fx};$$

  * \(F\) preserves composites: for all morphisms \(f:x\to y\) and \(g:y\to z\) in \(\mathcal C\),

$$F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff.$$

//Example 1.13.// We have the following examples of functors.

  * The forgetful functors \(U:\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\to\mathcal{Set}\), \(U:\mathcal{Vect}_k\to\mathcal{Set}\) and \(U:\mathcal{Top}\to\mathcal{Set}\) sending a pointed set, a \(k\)-vector space, or a topological space to its underlying set.
  * The functor \((-)_+:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\) which freely adjoins a basepoint to a set \(S\), namely \(S_+:=(S\amalg\{*\},*)\).
  * The functor \(\bigoplus_{(-)}k:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Vect}_k\) which sends a set \(S\) to the \(k\)-vector space with basis \(S\), namely \(\bigoplus_S k\).
  * The discrete topology functor \(D:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Top}\) equipping a set \(S\) with the discrete topology, namely \((S,\mathcal P(S))\), where \(\mathcal P(S)\) is the set of subsets of \(S\).
  * The indiscrete topology functor \(I:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Top}\) equipping a set \(S\) with the indiscrete topology, namely \((S,\{\emptyset,S\})\).

**Construction 1.19.** Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category and \(c\in\mathcal C\) be an object. There is a functor

$$\mathcal C(-,c):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set},$$

called the **representable functor** at \(c\), sending:

  * an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to the (small) set of morphisms \(\mathcal C(x,c)\);
  * a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to the function

$$f^*:\mathcal C(y,c)\to\mathcal C(x,c),\quad(g:y\to c)\mapsto(gf:x\to c).$$

This is a well-defined functor (Exercise).

**Construction 1.21.** Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category and \(f:c\to d\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal C\). There is a natural transformation

$$\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)$$

**Definition 1.22.** Given functors \(F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories, a natural transformation \(\alpha:F\Rightarrow G\) is a **natural isomorphism** if, for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\), its component \(\alpha_x:Fx\to Gx\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal D\).

We sometimes say that, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\), there is an isomorphism \(Fx\cong Gx\) which is **natural** in \(x\).

**Construction 1.23.** Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), there is a strict category \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), called the **functor strict category**, with

  * object set \(\operatorname{Ob}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)):=\mathcal{CAT}_s(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\) consisting of the functors \(\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\);
  * for all objects \(F,G\in\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), hom set \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)(F,G)\) consisting of the natural transformations \(F\Rightarrow G\);
  * for each object \(F\in\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), **identity natural transformation** \(\operatorname{id}_F:F\Rightarrow F\) having component at an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) given by

$$(\operatorname{id}_F)_c:=\operatorname{id}_{Fc}:Fc\to Fc;$$

  * for all morphisms \(\alpha:F\to G\) and \(\beta:G\to H\) in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), **composite natural transformation** \(\beta\circ\alpha:F\Rightarrow H\) having component at an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) given by the composite

$$(\beta\circ\alpha)_c:=\beta_c\circ\alpha_c:Fc\to Hc.$$

This is a well-defined strict category (Exercise).

**Construction 1.28.** Given a functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories and a strict category \(\mathcal E\), there is a functor

$$F^*:\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal E),$$

called the **precomposition functor** with \(F\), sending

  * a functor \(G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) to the composite \(GF:\mathcal C\to\mathcal E\);
  * a natural transformation \(\alpha:G\Rightarrow H\) between functors \(G,H:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) to the natural transformation \(\alpha F:GF\Rightarrow HF\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) is the morphism in \(\mathcal E\)

$$\alpha_{Fx}:G(Fx)\to H(Fx).$$

There is also a functor

$$F_*:\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal E,\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal E,\mathcal D),$$

called the **postcomposition functor** with \(F\), sending

  * a functor \(G:\mathcal E\to\mathcal C\) to the composite \(FG:\mathcal E\to\mathcal D\);
  * a natural transformation \(\alpha:G\Rightarrow H\) between functors \(G,H:\mathcal E\to\mathcal C\) to the natural transformation \(F\alpha:FG\Rightarrow FH\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal E\) is the morphism in \(\mathcal D\)

$$F(\alpha_x):F(Gx)\to F(Hx).$$

These are well-defined functors (Exercise).

**Theorem 2.1** (Yoneda lemma)**.** //Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. For all objects \(c\in\mathcal C\) and functors \(F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set}\), there is a bijection of sets//

$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F)\cong Fc$$

//which is natural in both \(c\) and \(F\).//

//Proof.// Evaluation at the identity morphism defines a function

$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F)\to Fc,\quad(\alpha:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F)\mapsto\alpha_c(\operatorname{id}_c),$$

where \(\alpha_c:\mathcal C(c,c)\to Fc\) is the function given by the component of \(\alpha\) at \(c\).

Next, consider the function

$$Fc\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F),\quad u\mapsto\alpha_u$$

sending an element \(u\in Fc\) to \(\alpha_u:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F\) with component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) given by the function

$$(\alpha_u)_x:\mathcal C(x,c)\to Fx,\quad(f:x\to c)\mapsto Ff(u),$$

where \(Ff:Fc\to Fx\) is the function given by the image of \(f\) under \(F\). This is a well-defined natural transformation (Exercise).

These functions are mutually inverse and natural in \(c\) and \(F\) (Exercise). \(\square\)
proof_dokuwiki:
//Proof.// Evaluation at the identity morphism defines a function

$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F)\to Fc,\quad(\alpha:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F)\mapsto\alpha_c(\operatorname{id}_c),$$

where \(\alpha_c:\mathcal C(c,c)\to Fc\) is the function given by the component of \(\alpha\) at \(c\).

Next, consider the function

$$Fc\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F),\quad u\mapsto\alpha_u$$

sending an element \(u\in Fc\) to \(\alpha_u:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F\) with component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) given by the function

$$(\alpha_u)_x:\mathcal C(x,c)\to Fx,\quad(f:x\to c)\mapsto Ff(u),$$

where \(Ff:Fc\to Fx\) is the function given by the image of \(f\) under \(F\). This is a well-defined natural transformation (Exercise).

These functions are mutually inverse and natural in \(c\) and \(F\) (Exercise). \(\square\)

**Construction 2.2.** Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. There is a functor

$$\mathsf y_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})$$

called the **Yoneda functor**, sending

  * an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) to the representable functor \(\mathcal C(-,c):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set}\);
  * a morphism \(f:c\to d\) in \(\mathcal C\) to the natural transformation \(\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)\).

**Definition 2.3.** A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is **fully faithful** if, for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), the induced function

$$\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)$$

is a bijection of sets.
statement_dokuwiki:
**Definition 2.3.** A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is **fully faithful** if, for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), the induced function

$$\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)$$

is a bijection of sets.

**Proposition 2.5.** //Let \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) be a fully faithful functor. Then \(F\) reflects isomorphisms, i.e., if \(f\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal C\) such that \(Ff\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal D\), then \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\).//

//Moreover, two objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\) are isomorphic if and only if their images \(Fx,Fy\in\mathcal D\) are isomorphic.//

proof_dokuwiki:
//Proof.// Since the Yoneda functor \(\mathsf y_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})\) is fully faithful, it preserves and reflects isomorphisms. Hence the morphism \(f:c\to d\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\) if and only if the natural transformation \(\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)\) is an isomorphism in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})\). By Proposition 1.24, this holds if and only if it is a natural isomorphism, i.e., for every object \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced morphism

$$f_*:\mathcal C(x,c)\to\mathcal C(x,d)$$

is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}\). This proves that (i) and (ii) are equivalent.

Next, observe that \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\) if and only if \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:d\to c\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) (Exercise). Then the equivalence between (i) and (ii) for \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) implies that \(f^{\mathrm{op}}\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) if and only if, for every object \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced morphism

$$f^{\mathrm{op}}_*=f^*:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}(x,d)=\mathcal C(d,x)\to\mathcal C(c,x)=\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}(x,c)$$

is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}\). This proves that (i) and (iii) are equivalent. \(\square\)

**Corollary 2.7.** //Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. Two objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\) are isomorphic if and only if their representable functors \(\mathcal C(-,x)\) and \(\mathcal C(-,y)\) are naturally isomorphic.//

//Proof.// This follows from the preceding proposition applied to the fully faithful Yoneda functor, together with Proposition 1.24. \(\square\)

//Example 3.2.// We have the following examples of adjunctions between strict categories.

  * The free-forgetful adjunctions

$$(-)_+:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}:U\quad\text{and}\quad\bigoplus_{(-)}k:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Vect}_k:U.$$

  * The discrete-forgetful and forgetful-indiscrete adjunctions

$$D:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Top}:U\quad\text{and}\quad U:\mathcal{Top}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Set}:I.$$

See Example 1.13 for the definition of the functors involved.

**Theorem 3.3** (Adjunctions representably)**.** //Given functors \(L:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) and \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) between strict categories, there is a unit and a counit making the pair \((L,R)\) into an adjunction \(L\dashv R\) if and only if, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\) and \(y\in\mathcal D\), there is a bijection//

$$\mathcal D(Lx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Ry)$$

//which is natural in \(x\) and \(y\).//

//Proof.// Given an adjunction \(L\dashv R\), the unit \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow RL\) induces a function

$$\mathcal D(Lx,y)\xrightarrow{R}\mathcal C(RLx,Ry)\xrightarrow{(\eta_x)^*}\mathcal C(x,Ry),\quad(g:Lx\to y)\mapsto R(g)\circ\eta_x,$$

and the counit \(\varepsilon:LR\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\) induces a function

$$\mathcal C(x,Ry)\xrightarrow{L}\mathcal D(Lx,LRy)\xrightarrow{(\varepsilon_y)_*}\mathcal D(Lx,y),\quad(f:x\to Ry)\mapsto\varepsilon_y\circ L(f).$$

These are mutually inverse and natural in \(x\) and \(y\) (Exercise).

Conversely, suppose that, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\) and \(y\in\mathcal D\), we are given natural bijections

$$\varphi_{x,y}:\mathcal D(Lx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Ry).$$

Define \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow RL\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) is given by

$$\eta_x:=\varphi_{x,Lx}(\operatorname{id}_{Lx}):x\to RLx.$$

Define \(\varepsilon:LR\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\) whose component at an object \(y\in\mathcal D\) is given by the morphism

$$\varepsilon_y:=\varphi^{-1}_{Ry,y}(\operatorname{id}_{Ry}):LRy\to y.$$

These are well-defined natural transformations satisfying the triangle identities (Exercise).

This proves that \(L\dashv R\) is an adjunction. \(\square\)

//Example 3.5.// The following classes of functors give special cases of equivalences.

  * Any isomorphism in \(\mathcal{CAT}_s\) is an equivalence of strict categories.
  * Given an adjunction \(L\dashv R\) such that the unit and the counit are natural isomorphisms, then both \(L\) and \(R\) are equivalences of strict categories; we refer to this as an **adjoint equivalence**.

Fact: every equivalence of strict categories can be promoted to an adjoint equivalence; see [Rie16, Corollary 4.3.6]. We won’t use this fact in this course.

verbatim_dokuwiki: **Construction 3.8.** The **walking isomorphism** is the strict category \(\mathcal I:=\{0\cong1\}\) with two objects \(0\) and \(1\), whose only morphisms are the identities and mutually inverse isomorphisms \(f:0\to1\) and \(f^{-1}:1\to0\). Observe that the hom sets of \(\mathcal I\) are all singletons.
statement_dokuwiki: **Construction 3.8.** The **walking isomorphism** is the strict category \(\mathcal I:=\{0\cong1\}\) with two objects \(0\) and \(1\), whose only morphisms are the identities and mutually inverse isomorphisms \(f:0\to1\) and \(f^{-1}:1\to0\). Observe that the hom sets of \(\mathcal I\) are all singletons.
**Proposition 3.9.** //The functor \(0:[0]\to\mathcal I\) is an equivalence of strict categories.//
proof_dokuwiki:
//Proof.// It is surjective on objects up to isomorphisms, since \(0\cong0\) in \(\mathcal I\), and it is fully faithful since, for the unique object \(*\in[0]\), we have a bijection

$$[0](*,*)=\{\operatorname{id}_*\}\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}\{\operatorname{id}_0\}=\mathcal I(0,0).\quad\square$$
